---
title: "4. Cast the System"
description: "Turn important responsibilities into characters with voice, personality, and relationship. Produce characters.md."
order: 4
---

## Overview

Characters are **not** arbitrary decoration. Each one represents a
responsibility in the system, and each line of dialogue is an explanation of a
system interaction. That is what makes the story teach rather than merely
entertain.

This lesson teaches you to turn responsibilities into characters. You will
produce a `characters.md` file that records each character's technical
counterpart, responsibility, personality, voice, and relationships.

## Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

- Convert a system responsibility into a character with a distinct personality and
  voice.
- Write `characters.md` with all required fields: Character, Technical
  counterpart, Responsibility, Personality, Voice, Relationship to other
  characters.
- Keep the cast small and distinct enough for audio-only identification.
- Apply the "breaking the fourth wall" technique when appropriate.

## Characters are responsibilities in disguise

Each character maps to a responsibility in the system. The Customer represents
the Developer's role of requesting an environment. The Chef represents the
engine that selects a recipe and composes the dish. The Manager represents
reconciliation — checking and re-checking until reality matches desire.

This mapping is what gives the story its teaching power. A line of dialogue
between two characters is a way of explaining a system interaction. Compare:

- **Narration:** "The developer creates a composite resource." (tells)
- **Dialogue:** "One application environment, please." / "Certainly. I'll use the
  recipe associated with that order." (shows the responsibility hand-off)

Dialogue carries the explanation. Narration handles connective tissue that has no
character voice.

## The characters.md format

For each character, record:

| Field | Description |
| --- | --- |
| Character | The name of the character in the story world. |
| Technical counterpart | Which entity or responsibility from `concept.md` it represents. |
| Responsibility | What the character does in the story (and what the technical entity does in the system). |
| Personality | The character's demeanour — how they come across to the listener. |
| Voice | The vocal quality or tone the listener will hear. |
| Relationship to other characters | How this character interacts with the rest of the cast. |

## The reference cast

The Crossplane restaurant uses five characters (plus a narrator). Read the
complete version under
[`reference-example/characters.md`](../../reference-example/characters.md).

| Character | Technical counterpart | Responsibility |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Customer | Developer | Requests a composite environment |
| Server | Claim (XRC) | Carries the request to the kitchen |
| Chef | Crossplane + Composition | Selects the recipe, composes the dish |
| Apprentice | Composition → MRs | Helps assemble the prepared components |
| Manager | Reconciliation | Checks and perfects the dish |

### Roles vs. things

Notice that a character may represent a **role or process** (Chef = the engine
and its recipe selection) rather than a single object. What matters is that the
listener can attach a name to each responsibility and follow the conversation.

## Dialogue as system interaction

Dialogue should *carry* the explanation. When the Customer says "I would like one
application environment," and the Chef replies "Certainly. I'll use the recipe
associated with that order," the listener learns that the engine consults a
recipe — without being told directly.

Prefer dialogue for the **relationships and state transitions** that matter most.
Reserve narration for connective tissue.

## Keeping the cast small

In audio drama, the listener has no visual cues to distinguish characters. Each
character must be identifiable by voice alone. This bounds the cast size — five
or six characters is typically the maximum a listener can track.

Every character must trace back to the mapping in `metaphor.md`. No character
should be introduced purely for comic effect without a responsibility behind it.
If a responsibility can be carried by an existing character, do not add a new one.

## Breaking the fourth wall

Occasionally a character may acknowledge its technical counterpart. This is an
**optional technique**, used sparingly, to re-anchor the listener when the
metaphor risks becoming so entertaining that they forget what each character
represents.

For example:

> **Chef:** Hello Developer — ahum, I mean *Customer*. What can I serve you
> today?

This reinforces the mapping between the story and the technical model without
abandoning the narrative.

Use it only when a re-anchor is genuinely needed. Overuse destroys immersion.

## Dialogue style: conversational form

Dialogue turns technical relationships into conversation. Instead of narrating
"the developer creates an XR," the characters speak to each other and the
responsibility hand-off becomes audible.

The response should expose a new responsibility the same way a system component
would. When the Chef says "I'll use the recipe associated with that order," the
listener learns about Composition without the word ever being defined.
